In order to herald in the new season, I decided to do a re-watch of Gatchaman Crowds, as well as watch its OVA, for the first time (btw, if you've seen GC, but not the OVA, go watch it; it illuminates some things about the ending).

Gatchaman Crowds is an oddball. I'll get that out of the way right now. The premise is essentially that there are these superheroes, called Gatchaman, that protect the Earth from aliens. They have pocketbooks, called NOTES, which allow them to transform into their mecha-like Gatchaman suits, which obviously have powers. The show opens with our main character, Ichinose Hajime, who is granted the powers of Gatchaman by the mysterious, transcendental being, JJ-sama. Sounds like a slightly weirder-than-normal anime, right? Something that is probably about average, no? The truth is, Gatchaman Crowds isn't about aliens or mecha superhero things, and the show doesn't let on until about four episodes in.

What makes Gatchaman Crowds stand out is its sometimes-confusing commentary. This anime is likely a product of its era, and will probably not be remembered by time. However, GC is incredibly relevant, right now, in this transitionary age we live in. Gatchaman Crowds explores the duality of human nature, the inefficiency of human systems, and the possibilities of human technologies. Gatchaman Crowds seeks to reconcile the old, beurocratic, and inefficient ways of society with the new, more democratic, more digital, and more anonymous world, which we are coming into. At the same time, this anime seeks to test the volatile human soul in order to spell out the dangers and hopeful possibilities of the new world. If we were to boil down the aim of Gatchaman Crowds, it would be to show us both the empathetic and destructive sides of humanity, and how our most potent tool, the Internet, amplifies these.

I still have not gotten to why Gatchaman Crowds is such an amazing anime. Rather than exclusively portray the disgusting inhumanity of mankind, which so many shows in its position would be apt to do, Gatchaman Crowds offers a more hopeful message. A statement that, despite the evil that lurks within us all, there is hope for a brighter tomorrow. This is why I love Gatchaman Crowds.

As I mentioned before, this anime takes a while to set itself up, and it's not even apparent that it's doing so until about episode four. Even then, I didn't realize a lot of what the show was doing in those first few episodes until my second viewing. Other downsides would be the very strange slant on voice acting (you'll know what I mean when you watch it), the very exaggerated personality of the MC, and the CG Gatchaman suits (though these are pulled of decently). If you can get past those, then you have a fun story, a relevant message, and a killer soundtrack to enjoy. This show isn't perfect, but it definitely rates towards the top.
